paragraphs.text: Microwave doors: what explains metal mesh?

Start with the detail itself. Look closely at a microwave door: there's a metal mesh. It is not decoration. It is part of the shield. The oven works as a Faraday cage that keeps the energy inside. The holes in the mesh are much smaller than the wavelength of the microwaves. So the microwaves cannot pass through the door. Visible light has a far shorter wavelength, so it passes straight through. That is why you can watch your food while the energy stays in.

The documentation makes the purpose clearer. The governing physics: The holes in the conductive mesh are much smaller than the wavelength of the microwaves, so the door is part of the oven's Faraday cage. The door of a microwave oven usually has a window with a layer of conductive mesh to maintain the shielding. The perforations in the mesh are much smaller than the microwaves' wavelength, so microwave radiation cannot pass through the door while visible light can. A microwave oven uses a Faraday cage, partly visible covering the window, to contain the electromagnetic energy within the oven. Microwaves are produced inside the oven by an electron tube called a magnetron. A federal standard limits the amount of microwaves that can leak from an oven throughout its lifetime to 5 milliwatts of microwave radiation per square centimeter at approximately 2 inches from the oven surface. Microwave ovens shall have at least two operative safety interlocks.
But one detail complicates the familiar story. The mesh looks like a decorative screen, but it is part of the shielding that keeps the energy inside.
The design did not stop changing there. Microwaves cannot pass through the door, while visible light passes through the window.
